policy: Individually measured stellar companions of pulsars in the compact-remnant overlay. Each value comes from the cited paper; nothing is copied from the pulsar except its system position and astrometry, which the companion shares. Upper limits are kept in notes, not stored as measurements. The luminous stars of the dormant compact-object systems in the compact-remnant overlay, with each physical value from the cited discovery paper. A star shares its system's plotted position and the reviewed system astrometry of the unresolved binary. The visible stars of X-ray and gamma-ray binaries, of Gaia BH2 and of pulsars with a recorded optical counterpart or a main-sequence companion in the compact-remnant overlay, with each value from the cited paper. A value stays empty when no individual measurement was verified; none is inferred from a mass ratio. Very low-mass, ablated black-widow companions are classed as brown dwarfs.

psr-j0437m4715-b.note: Helium white dwarf seen in optical and infrared spectra; its hydrogen-atmosphere fit gives log g = 6.98 ± 0.15.

psr-j1012p5307-b.note: Low-mass helium-core white dwarf with Balmer absorption lines (DA; van Kerkwijk et al. 1996).

psr-j1614m2230-b.note: Mass from the Shapiro delay; ATNF classifies the companion as a carbon–oxygen white dwarf.

psr-j2222m0137-b.note: Optical non-detection limits its effective temperature to below 3000 K (Kaplan et al. 2014, https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.0488), making it one of the coolest white dwarfs known.

gaia-bh1-b.note: A slowly rotating, Sun-like G dwarf whose motion reveals the unseen black hole.

gaia-bh3-b.note: An old, very metal-poor giant of the Galactic halo (log g = 2.929 ± 0.003) whose motion reveals the unseen black hole.

gaia-ns1-b.note: A lithium-rich, metal-poor halo star near the main-sequence turnoff. Its motion reveals the unseen neutron-star candidate. Temperature, radius, luminosity, mass and age are the paper's SED fit.

gaia-bh2-b.note: A low-luminosity, slightly metal-poor red giant enhanced in alpha elements; it reveals the unseen black hole through its orbit.

a0620-00-b.note: A K-type donor star feeding the black hole; the 4600 K temperature is the value adopted in the mass analysis.

xte-j1118p480-b.note: A cool dwarf donor; its K7 V to M1 V spectral type is from near-infrared spectroscopy (Khargharia et al. 2013, https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.2786).

cygnus-x-1-b.note: The blue supergiant HDE 226868, whose wind feeds the black hole; the published mass interval is +7.7/-7.1 M_sun and the larger side is stored.

v404-cygni-b.note: A K-type giant losing gas to the black hole; its spectral type is from near-infrared spectroscopy (Khargharia et al. 2010, https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.5358). A wider third star also belongs to the system.

gro-j0422p32-b.note: A small M-type donor; its M1 spectral type is from Gelino & Harrison 2003, https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0308490.

gs-2000p25-b.note: A K-type dwarf donor, as listed by Casares & Jonker 2014, https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.5118.

maxi-j1820p070-b.note: A subgiant donor. Its temperature is about 4200 K at the system's distance; the published lower limit is 4200 K.

scorpius-x-1-b.note: A low-mass donor star, first caught through narrow emission lines from its X-ray-lit face (Steeghs & Casares 2002, https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0107343).

centaurus-x-4-b.note: A spotted K-type dwarf with 0.1755 times the neutron star's mass; K4 V and 4500 K are from González Hernández et al. 2005, as cited.

vela-x-1-b.note: The blue supergiant HD 77581, whose wind feeds the neutron star (Kretschmar et al. 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.13148).

x-persei-b.note: The Be star that gives the system its name. Its mass is the midpoint of the 13-20 M_sun range the source lists.

a0535p26-b.note: A Be star whose gas disk feeds the neutron star's outbursts (Caballero et al. 2011, https://arxiv.org/abs/1107.3417); its spectral type is SIMBAD's.

ls-i-61-303-b.note: A rapidly rotating B0 Ve star (Weng et al. 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.09423).

v404-cygni-c.note: An evolved star at least 3,500 AU from the inner binary, 1.43 arcseconds away on the sky. Its evolved state dates the system to 3-5 Gyr; its plotted position is the system's. Its mass comes from isochrones.

psr-j1023p0038-b.note: A low-mass star that has fed the pulsar on and off; this is a transitional system moving between pulsar and X-ray binary states (Deller et al. 2012, https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.5670).

psr-j1024m0719-b.note: A low-metallicity star on a very long orbit, published as 2,000 to 20,000 years.

psr-j2129m0429-b.note: An optically bright redback companion with mean r-band magnitude 16.6 (Bellm et al. 2016, https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00721).

psr-j1036m4353-b.note: A redback companion identified optically (Phosrisom et al. 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.06503).

psr-j1723m2837-b.note: An eclipsing redback companion. Its mass is the midpoint of the published 0.4-0.7 M_sun range.

psr-j2039m5617-b.note: A redback companion with long-term optical variability (Clark et al. 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.14849). Its mass is the midpoint of the 0.15-0.22 M_sun range quoted.

psr-j1227m4853-b.note: The companion of a transitional redback pulsar (Johnson et al. 2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.06862).

psr-j1740m5340a-b.note: A metal-poor “red straggler” in the globular cluster NGC 6397, from a high-resolution spectrum and Hubble photometry.

psr-j1740m5340b-b.note: A companion in NGC 6397 that has probably just left the main sequence and begun transferring mass (Zhang et al. 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07880).

psr-j1302m6350-b.note: The Be star LS 2883, oblate from fast rotation: its equator is near 27,500 K and its poles near 34,000 K, with an equatorial radius of 9.7 R_sun and a polar radius of 8.1 R_sun.

psr-j2032p4127-b.note: The Be star MT91 213 in the Cygnus OB2 association.

psr-j1431m4715-b.note: A redback companion, studied with optical spectroscopy (Strader et al. 2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.04626).

psr-j2339m0533-b.note: A strongly heated redback companion: its visible side varies from about 6900 K to below 3000 K across the orbit (Romani & Shaw 2011, https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.3074), and it has hot spots, likely magnetic poles, that move over the years (Kandel et al. 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.04105).

psr-j0212p5321-b.note: An F6-type star tidally distorted by the pulsar; the type is Linares et al. 2017 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02232). The published mass interval is +0.22/-0.19 M_sun and the larger side is stored.

psr-j0838m2827-b.note: A heated companion of spectral type M1 or later (Halpern et al. 2017, https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.09511).

psr-j2302p4442-b.note: A He- or CO-core white dwarf identified optically at r = 23.33. Published intervals are +0.25/-0.19 M_sun and +1000/-800 K; the larger sides are stored.

psr-j0337p1715-b.note: The inner of the pulsar's two white dwarfs: hot and low-gravity, with log g = 5.82 ± 0.05. Its outer white dwarf has 0.40962 M_sun but no optical detection.

psr-j1738p0333-b.note: A low-mass white dwarf with a thick hydrogen envelope, bright enough for spectroscopy. The published interval is +0.007/-0.005 M_sun and the larger side is stored.

psr-j2317p1439-b.note: A white dwarf with a cooling age of 10.9 ± 0.3 Gyr. Published intervals are +0.13/-0.10 M_sun and +550/-470 K; the larger sides are stored.

psr-j1400m1431-b.note: A cool DA white dwarf; its radius scales with the assumed distance.

psr-j1741p1351-b.note: Probably a He-core white dwarf, matching the mass from radio timing.

psr-j0348p0432-b.note: A white dwarf with very low mass, whose spectroscopy set the system's mass ratio.

psr-j0023p0923-b.note: A black-widow companion: a very low-mass object heated by the pulsar and seen optically (Breton et al. 2013, https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.1790).

psr-j2256m1024-b.note: A black-widow companion: a very low-mass object heated by the pulsar and seen optically (Breton et al. 2013, https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.1790).

psr-j0610m2100-b.note: A black-widow companion irradiated by the pulsar, tentatively a heavily ablated very low-mass star (van der Wateren et al. 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.05872).

psr-j2214p3000-b.note: A black-widow companion modelled from its optical light curve (Schroeder & Halpern 2014, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.7966).

psr-j1959p2048-b.note: The original black-widow companion, heated on its pulsar-facing side and cooler than about 2800 K on its far side (Fruchter et al. 1995, https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9502084). The pulsar outweighs it 69.2 ± 0.8 times (van Kerkwijk et al. 2011, https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.5427).
